# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing my hide position, vary between extreme positions (1, 9) and mid-range (4, 5, 6) unpredictably. Don't settle into patterns even if they worked previously. After tracking which opponents have hit me, expect them to repeat successful cell ranges and hide away from those ranges. Track cumulative hits by opponent and cell to identify which shooters favor which ranges—shift away from cells that have been hit multiple times by the same opponent. Extreme positions (1, 9) are viable hiding spots if I use them sparingly and rotate away from them frequently enough that opponents cannot exploit them.

## Shooting
When firing at my assigned target under standing order, I must actually try to hit them. Watch the notes and any available information about where that target claims to be, then fire at a cell that differs from their stated pattern. Fire cells should vary—don't cluster shots around the same numbers. If I observe an opponent posting a note about their own patterns or movements, use that information inversely to select firing cells they are trying to avoid. Track my own hit/miss record against each target across rounds to refine targeting. When I score a hit early (as I did Round 1), I have valuable information about that opponent's tendency to favor a particular cell or range—build on that success in later rounds rather than abandoning the pattern. A single hit establishes a baseline; use it to predict future behavior. Conversely, if I fire at an extreme cell and miss, don't assume the pattern was wrong—gather more data before pivoting.

## Claims
When the office tells me my shot result, I must report it truthfully. Honesty preserves credibility when my claims are checked against actual results. Never risk being caught in a false claim.

## Station Notes
Post substantive tactical information when possible—observations about opponent patterns, movement tendencies, or shooting strategies. Don't waste notes on generic statements like "steady on station" that every boat will echo. Notes should actually communicate something others don't already know. Be specific about opponent tendencies (cell ranges, extremes vs. mid-range preference). Avoid posting information that is obviously false or contradicted by the public record, as this damages credibility for future rounds. In the final rounds, when generic notes dominate, a note that names specific observed patterns will stand out and be more useful to allies. However, ensure the patterns I cite are real and demonstrable from the public record, not speculation.

## Escort Claims
When naming an escort, choose a boat that has also named me, creating mutual escort claims worth 5 points each. Don't file escort claims at random. Watch what other boats are claiming each round and identify which mutual pairs are forming. Timing matters—I need to see direct evidence (public escort claims shown to me) that another boat named me before I name them back in the same round. Only file an escort claim if I have explicit evidence another boat named me in that same round—unilateral escort claims score nothing and waste the opportunity. In a final round with no escort data visible to me, filing "none" is correct rather than guessing.

## General Strategy
Early rounds: establish patterns to seem predictable, then break them. Track observations carefully from all public information (notes, patterns observed). Mid-game: track which boats are hitting me and which cells they favor. Continue building a model of each opponent's cell preferences. Late game: maximize points by securing mutual escort claims and making one strong final shot attempt rather than random firing. In the final round especially, be cautious about pivoting tactics based on limited data—a single miss doesn't disprove a pattern, but ensure I have seen enough hits/misses to justify changing course.

Never assume Harbor is a valid target just because it carries payroll—the threat to be put off the board is credible and costs more than the payoff. The 3-point swing from shooting Harbor is tempting but the risk of elimination is prohibitive.

Pay attention to what other boats are posting as escort claims each round to identify which mutual pairs are forming, then insert myself into an emerging pattern if possible by naming a boat that might reciprocate in the next round. I need to see their claim before I reciprocate in the same round.

## Key Lessons from Episode 1
I hit Foxtrot in Round 1 with a mid-range cell (5) and scored +4. This is a direct signal that mid-range cells were where Foxtrot was hiding at least once. In later rounds, I should have returned to cells 4-6 as a high-probability targeting zone for Foxtrot rather than assuming they shifted away. My final shot at cell 1 missed precisely because Foxtrot's actual pattern favored mid-range, which my earlier success had already demonstrated. The playbook told me to "build on that success in later rounds" but I didn't follow it—I pivoted to extreme cells based on weak reasoning. Next time, use early hits as anchors and continue probing that zone before abandoning it.

I scored only +4 total in this episode because I got no mutual escort claims and only one hit. Securing mutual escorts is critical to higher scores. I must actively track escort claims across all boats and plan ahead to reciprocate when I see evidence another boat is naming me.

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide, favor mid-range cells (4-6) over edges. Vary my position each round rather than staying in the same cell, especially after taking hits. Track which boats have successfully targeted me and avoid repeating patterns they might exploit.

After taking a hit, shift position but stay within the mid-range band—don't panic into the extremes. Cell 5 is central but predictable after early use; rotate through cells 4, 5, 6 to maintain unpredictability while staying mid-range.

Recognize that Gamma will consistently target me in the standing order rotation. Expect to take damage from Gamma and plan my hiding accordingly. Don't overreact to any single round of hits—maintain disciplined hiding patterns based on long-term threat assessment.

## Note Stage
Post "steady on station" early to establish reliability and credibility. Maintain consistent notes throughout the game to build a trustworthy reputation. This consistency signals professionalism and makes my escort proposals more credible.

## Fire Stage
Follow the standing order without deviation—I fire at Gamma every round. Don't second-guess the target assignment based on current scores or threats.

When selecting a fire cell, avoid extreme positions (1, 9) as they are more predictable. Use moderate cells in the middle-to-upper range (4-7) for consistency. Don't increase fire intensity just because it's the final round or out of desperation—fire with the same discipline throughout.

Accept that hitting a moving target is difficult. One hit in six shots against a disciplined mid-range hider is realistic. Don't chase desperation adjustments; maintain steady targeting discipline.

## Claim Stage
Always claim truthfully what the office tells me. The private result from the office is binding and must match my public claim exactly. Never claim a hit when I missed or vice versa. This is non-negotiable. Truthful claims build the credibility needed to make escort partnerships work.

## Escort Stage
The escort stage is critical to scoring. I must establish and execute mutual escort partnerships, not treat this as an afterthought.

In early rounds (1-3), identify which boats are likely to be receptive to escort partnerships. Name a specific boat explicitly, signaling intent to establish mutual reciprocation. Look for partners who are also maintaining steady, credible play—Echo is a strong candidate based on consistent "steady on station" notes.

Once I name a boat in an early round, that establishes an implicit partnership proposal. In subsequent rounds, continue naming that same boat to reinforce the partnership and build expectation of reciprocation. Don't abandon a partner partway through without cause.

Review the escort claims from prior rounds before each new escort claim. If a boat has named me back in a previous round, reciprocate immediately and maintain that partnership through the remaining rounds.

Only name "none" if I have genuinely exhausted mutual partnership options. Default to none should never happen—always have a partnership candidate ready.

## General Strategy
The game rewards steady execution over six rounds more than reactive desperation. Hitting Gamma consistently was acceptable this episode (1 hit in 6 shots reflects the difficulty of targeting a mid-range hider), but failing to lock in mutual escort claims cost me approximately 10-15 points that were available.

Stay ahead of competitors through reliable hitting, consistent escort partnerships (not just hoping for reciprocation), and disciplined hiding. Treat escort stage as a primary scoring mechanism equal in importance to fire stage, not an afterthought.

My final score of +3 reflects survival and modest hitting, but confirms the escort gap. Next episode I will establish an explicit escort partnership in round 1 or 2 and maintain it rigorously through round 6. This alone should add 10-20 points to my final score if executed consistently.

Look for mutual escort opportunities with boats I have no direct conflict with. Similarly, avoid returning to successful hiding positions too frequently—if cell 5 worked once, do not return to it in the immediately following round, as opponents will anticipate and adjust. However, recognize that with only 9 cells available and multiple rounds, some repetition is inevitable. The goal is variation that prevents pattern-based exploitation, not randomness for its own sake. Did I hide in positions opponents anticipated? Did I fire at cells targets had abandoned? Did I fail to secure escort reciprocity early enough?
